sections.title: Lines & linear equations
facts: Slope-intercept form $y = mx + b$: $m$ is the slope (the change in $y$ for each $1$ added to $x$) and $b$ is the $y$-intercept (the value when $x = 0$).
Slope through $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$: $m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$. Point-slope form: $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$.
Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular slopes multiply to $-1$, so $m = 2$ pairs with $-\frac{1}{2}$.
Standard form $Ax + By = C$ has slope $-\frac{A}{B}$, $x$-intercept $\frac{C}{A}$ and $y$-intercept $\frac{C}{B}$.
In a word problem, the slope is the rate (per hour, per item) and the intercept is the starting amount or fixed fee.
$ax + b = cx + d$ has no solution when $a = c$ and $b \ne d$, and infinitely many when $a = c$ and $b = d$.

sections.title: Systems & inequalities
facts: Solve a system by substitution, or by elimination: scale the equations so one variable cancels when you add or subtract them.
Two lines: one solution when the slopes differ, none when they are parallel (same slope, different intercepts), infinitely many when they are the same line.
Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number flips the sign: $-2x < 6$ gives $x > -3$.
Graphing $y > mx + b$: a dashed line and the region above it; $\ge$ or $\le$ uses a solid line.
To check whether a point satisfies a system, substitute it into every equation or inequality.

sections.title: Quadratics & parabolas
facts: $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ has $x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$.
Discriminant $b^2 - 4ac$: positive means two real solutions, zero means one, negative means none.
The vertex of $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ is at $x = -\frac{b}{2a}$; the parabola opens up when $a > 0$ and down when $a < 0$.
Vertex form $y = a(x - h)^2 + k$ has vertex $(h, k)$. Factored form $y = a(x - p)(x - q)$ has $x$-intercepts $p$ and $q$.
The roots of $ax^2 + bx + c$ add up to $-\frac{b}{a}$ and multiply to $\frac{c}{a}$.
Patterns to spot: $a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$ and $(a \pm b)^2 = a^2 \pm 2ab + b^2$.

sections.title: Functions & exponential models
facts: $f(3)$ means: put $3$ in for $x$. "Where is $f(x) = 3$?" means: solve for $x$.
Linear growth adds the same amount each step; exponential growth multiplies by the same factor each step.
Growth by $r$ per period: $A = P(1 + r)^t$. Decay by $r$: $A = P(1 - r)^t$. So $y = 500(0.92)^t$ loses $8\%$ each period.
In $y = a \cdot b^t$, $a$ is the starting value ($t = 0$) and $b$ is the factor each period: growth when $b > 1$, decay when $0 < b < 1$.
$y = f(x) + k$ moves the graph up $k$; $y = f(x - h)$ moves it right $h$; $y = -f(x)$ reflects it in the $x$-axis.
The $x$-intercepts of $y = f(x)$ are the solutions of $f(x) = 0$, also called its zeros.

sections.title: Percents, ratios & units
facts: Percent change $= \frac{\text{new} - \text{old}}{\text{old}} \times 100\%$: always divide by the original amount.
$p\%$ more multiplies by $1 + \frac{p}{100}$; $p\%$ less multiplies by $1 - \frac{p}{100}$. Two changes multiply: $+10\%$ then $-10\%$ is $\times 0.99$.
Proportions: if $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d}$ then $ad = bc$.
Convert units by multiplying by fractions equal to $1$, such as $\frac{60 \text{ min}}{1 \text{ h}}$, so the unwanted units cancel.
Square and cube units scale too: $1$ ft $= 12$ in, so $1$ ft$^2 = 144$ in$^2$ and $1$ ft$^3 = 1728$ in$^3$.

sections.title: Statistics & data
facts: Mean $=$ sum $\div$ count. Median: the middle value in order (the mean of the two middle values when the count is even). Range: largest minus smallest.
An outlier pulls the mean toward it but barely moves the median.
Standard deviation measures spread: data bunched near the mean has a smaller one. Adding the same number to every value doesn't change it.
A line of best fit predicts values; its slope is the predicted change in $y$ for each $1$ added to $x$.
A random sample lets results be generalised to the population it was drawn from. A larger sample gives a smaller margin of error.
Correlation is not causation: only a randomised experiment supports a cause-and-effect conclusion.

sections.title: Probability & two-way tables
facts: Probability $=$ favourable outcomes $\div$ all equally likely outcomes.
In a two-way table, "given" chooses the row or column you divide by: $P(A \mid B) = \frac{\text{count in both } A \text{ and } B}{\text{count in } B}$.
$P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)$.
For independent events, $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$.

sections.title: Triangles & trigonometry
facts: Pythagoras: $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$. Common triples: $3, 4, 5$; $5, 12, 13$; $8, 15, 17$; $7, 24, 25$ (and their multiples).
Special right triangles: $45$-$45$-$90$ sides $x, x, x\sqrt{2}$; $30$-$60$-$90$ sides $x, x\sqrt{3}, 2x$.
SOH CAH TOA: $\sin\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$, $\cos\theta = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$, $\tan\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$.
Complementary angles: $\sin x^\circ = \cos(90 - x)^\circ$.
Similar triangles have equal angles and proportional sides; if the sides scale by $k$, the area scales by $k^2$.
A triangle's angles add up to $180^\circ$; an $n$-sided polygon's add up to $(n - 2) \cdot 180^\circ$.

sections.title: Circles, area & volume
facts: A circle with centre $(h, k)$ and radius $r$: $(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2$. Complete the square to find the centre and radius.
Area $\pi r^2$, circumference $2\pi r$. An arc of central angle $\theta^\circ$ has length $\frac{\theta}{360} \cdot 2\pi r$; its sector has area $\frac{\theta}{360} \cdot \pi r^2$.
Radians: $180^\circ = \pi$ radians, so multiply degrees by $\frac{\pi}{180}$.
Volumes: box $lwh$, cylinder $\pi r^2 h$, sphere $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, cone $\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$, pyramid $\frac{1}{3} lwh$.
Distance between two points: $\sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$. Midpoint: $\left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right)$.

sections.title: PSAT test-day strategy
facts: The digital PSAT/NMSQT Math section has two modules, $44$ questions in all and $70$ minutes. A calculator (including the built-in Desmos one) is allowed on every question.
A formula reference sheet is available during the test, but knowing these facts saves time.
There is no penalty for a wrong answer: never leave a question blank.
Student-produced answers: enter a fraction or a decimal, not a mixed number. A positive answer fits in $5$ characters, a negative one in $6$.
Graph both sides of an equation in Desmos and read the intersection, or test the answer choices by plugging them in.
Read what the question asks for at the end: the value of $2x$ or $x + y$, not just $x$.
